entry.title: Debezium 3.7.0.CR1 Released

link.title: Debezium 3.7.0.CR1 Released

entry.content:
With autumn officially underway, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.0.CR1, the first release candidate for the 3.7 series, focused on stability and polish ahead of the final release.

Among the highlights, PyDebeziumAI brings real-time change data capture to LangChain and LangGraph applications, the Oracle connector gains new tools for monitoring and troubleshooting long-running transactions, and MongoDB now keeps streaming from the preferred replica set member after a failover. This release also includes important reliability fixes for MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, and Oracle, along with numerous other improvements across the board.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.7.0.CR1

Debezium for Oracle

Last enqueued event tracking moved to the transaction cache

The buffered LogMiner implementation now tracks the most recently enqueued event for each transaction directly in the transaction cache, rather than in a separate structure maintained alongside it. This consolidates transaction state in a single place, reducing duplicated bookkeeping in the streaming pipeline.

To support this, the XML begin and end events now carry the redo sequence number (SEQUENCE#), which the connector uses to detect the boundary between statements that contain XML updates when handling rollbacks. As a result, the serialized form of these events stored in the Ehcache and Infinispan transaction buffers has changed.

If you use the Ehcache or Infinispan buffer types and capture XMLTYPE columns, allow any in-flight transactions to complete and clear the transaction buffer caches before upgrading, as XML events persisted by an earlier version cannot be deserialized. Deployments using the default heap buffer are not affected. (dbz#2652)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium Platform

Debezium AI for Python

Debezium for MongoDB

Read preference honored after replica set promotion

The connector now continues to respect the configured read preference when a replica set member it is streaming from changes role. Previously, when a secondary serving the change stream was promoted to primary, the connector kept streaming from that node, placing unwanted load on the primary.

The connector now monitors the replica set topology, and when a promotion invalidates the read preference, it closes the change stream cursor, reopens it against a node matching the read preference, and resumes from the last resume token. This completes the remaining work for reading changes from MongoDB secondaries and helps keep streaming load off the primary. (dbz#917)

Debezium for Oracle

Total abandoned transaction count metric

The Oracle LogMiner JMX metrics now include a TotalAbandonedTransactionCount metric that increments every time a transaction is abandoned. The existing metrics expose abandoned transactions as an array of transaction identifiers, which is impractical to scrape and chart in tools such as Prometheus and Grafana. The new counter makes it easy to monitor and alert on abandoned transactions over time. (dbz#2428)

Richer in-flight transaction logging

When the buffered LogMiner implementation logs transactions that have not yet committed or rolled back, it now includes additional metadata about each transaction, such as its creation time and the number of buffered events, rather than only the transaction identifier and SCN. This gives administrators the details they need to make an informed decision about dropping a long-running transaction without having to run manual LogMiner queries.

When deferred transactions are in use, the state of the deferred transactions is also logged as a separate entry, using the same format. (dbz#2576)

Signal to log pending transactions

A new signal lets you dump the connector’s current view of active and deferred transactions to the connector logs on demand. Previously, obtaining this information required additional logging that may not have been enabled at the time, or direct access to query LogMiner.

For each transaction, the output includes the transaction identifier, starting SCN, change time, username, client identifier, redo thread, and, for active transactions, the number of buffered events. Entries are sorted from oldest to newest, making it easy to identify which transactions are holding back the mining window and to pair the output with the existing drop-transaction signal. (dbz#2577)

ORA-02002 treated as a retriable error

The connector now treats ORA-02002 as a retriable error. During a switchover or failover with multiple archive destinations configured, Oracle can raise ORA-02002: error while writing to audit trail, which previously caused the connector to stop unexpectedly. The connector now retries in this scenario, allowing it to recover automatically once the failover completes. (dbz#2625)

Debezium Platform

Custom evaluation window for alert rules

When creating an alert rule, the Evaluation window field now offers a Custom option in addition to the predefined set of durations, allowing any window between 1 and 60 minutes to be entered. This gives users the flexibility to tune alert rules to the exact time window that suits their pipelines. (dbz#2563)

Debezium AI for Python

PyDebeziumAI for real-time RAG with LangChain and LangGraph

PyDebeziumAI is a new Python library that integrates directly with Debezium to keep vector stores in sync with your relational database in real time. As rows change, it automatically updates the corresponding embeddings, so retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and LLM agents always work with current data.

The library consumes Debezium change events either in embedded mode or as JSON from a message broker, maps them into LangChain-compatible documents with configurable projection of columns into content and metadata, and uses deterministic identifiers to apply correct upsert and delete semantics to the vector index. It includes out-of-the-box adapters for Chroma, PGVector, and Milvus, support for soft deletes, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and a dead-letter queue for reliable delivery.

LangChain-compatible retrievers and LangGraph node integrations allow LLM agents to work directly with the synchronized data. The project, including end-to-end RAG examples, is available in the debezium-ai-python repository. (dbz#2066)

Other fixes

  • Improve the initial loading state management in the Platform UI (dbz#1725)

  • CDC events missing and connector crash on a delete operation (dbz#1862)

  • Missing validation that tasks.min must be less than or equal to tasks.max (dbz#1870)

  • Validation issues with the JDBC connection for offset storage (dbz#1957)

  • Simplify the LogMiner buffered implementation event logic (dbz#1960)

  • Stream ongoing changes from the CDC log with a clean snapshot handoff (dbz#2160)

  • Add the SQL trigger generator that populates the CDC log (dbz#2161)

  • JDBC sink UNNEST batch writes fail when a batch contains multiple events for the same primary key (dbz#2356)

  • Connector silently loses rows after a keepalive reconnect under backpressure (dbz#2359)

  • Add a relational to Neo4j example to the debezium-examples repository (dbz#2453)

  • DDL parser fails on CREATE INDEX with the ONLINE keyword and on XMLTYPE with the SCHEMA feature (dbz#2484, dbz#2656)

  • Stage signal collection verification reports success when the collection does not exist (dbz#2526)

  • Wire format detection and snapshot consistency (dbz#2530)

  • Cassandra 5 CDC NullPointerException on ALTER TABLE enabling CDC on a pre-existing table (dbz#2541)

  • The internal custom.retriable.exception property is defined with a non-String default (dbz#2556)

  • Standby connector silently skips events after DDL changes (dbz#2598)

  • LogFileCollector exception is misleading when the archiver is slow to archive logs (dbz#2601)

  • MySQL and MariaDB error handlers pass a null throwable to super.isRetriable(), making every error non-retriable (dbz#2611)

  • Startup validation rejects valid split-event resume tokens (dbz#2619)

  • FieldToEmbedding uses shared static factory state and OpenAiModelFactory hardcodes request/response logging (dbz#2627)

  • Form values not visible in Alert Rules view mode when using dark mode (dbz#2629)

  • Conductor crashes with the chart default QUARKUS_MAILER_HOST="" (dbz#2630)

  • ExtractChangedRecordState reports false positives on unchanged binary fields and throws DataException on schema evolution (dbz#2635)

  • Log a warning that incremental snapshots are disabled for Oracle read-only mode (dbz#2637)

  • Fix typo in a comment in AbstractSnapshotChangeEventSource#execute (dbz#2638)

  • Stabilize incremental snapshot pause/resume test assertions (dbz#2641)

  • Fix false positives in the replica set authentication test (dbz#2643)

  • Guardrail test can stop the engine before startup completes (dbz#2645)

  • Do not fail on zero-year dates in MySQL (part II) (dbz#2659)

  • Test binlog client pull requests against the Debezium binlog connectors (dbz#2665)

  • SQL Server arithmetic overflow on tables with more than 2.14B rows during parallel chunked snapshot due to hardcoded COUNT(1) (dbz#2670)

  • ExtendedStringParser assigns schema and table names in reverse order (dbz#2671)

  • SelectLobParser.reset() does not reset the inherited parser state (dbz#2672)

  • Include source state and recent Connect logs in JDBC end-to-end startup timeouts (dbz#2684)

In total, 50 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.7.0.CR1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:

Blom, Akshat Sapra, Anilabha Baral, Bhuvan Somisetty, Charles Morgan, Chris Cranford, Dario Rodrigues, Gaétan Collaud, Garib Karimli, Giovanni Panice, Indra Shukla, Jiri Pechanec, Mario Fiore Vitale, Matt Langley, Minjae Lee, Philippe Camus, Robert Roldan, Sergei Nikolaev, Stanislav Deviatov, Sujal Shrestha, Thiago Garcia, and Virag Tripathi!

entry.title: Debezium 3.6.3.Final Released

link.title: Debezium 3.6.3.Final Released

entry.content:
We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.3.Final, a maintenance release focused on stability and reliability improvements.

The Oracle connector receives the most attention in this release, with corrected savepoint partial rollback handling for tables with LOB columns, a fix for unbounded mining sessions with the log-count mining algorithm, and ORA-02002 now treated as a retriable error so the connector can recover from failovers. The MySQL and MariaDB connectors once again restart automatically after transient communication errors, while the SQL Server, Vitess, and Informix connectors pick up targeted fixes ranging from ambiguous column name errors to irregular heartbeat intervals. If you use the Oracle connector with an Ehcache or Infinispan buffer, be sure to review the breaking changes before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.6.3.Final

Debezium for Oracle

Savepoint partial rollbacks handled correctly

The Oracle connector now correctly handles transactions that roll back to a savepoint, most notably for tables with LOB columns. Several defects in this area could cause the target to drift out of sync with the source, either by emitting changes that had been rolled back or by silently dropping changes that had not.

When LOB support is enabled, the connector consolidates related INSERT and UPDATE events for the same row, but this consolidation only carried the column values forward and left the merged INSERT with a placeholder row identifier. When the partial rollback arrived, the connector could not find the event to discard, logged a "Cannot undo" warning, and emitted the rolled-back change that looked like a normal change to the target.

Additionally, when a rollback-to-savepoint event was mined near the end of a LogMiner session for a transaction that had not yet committed, the same rollback could be applied a second time when the transaction’s events were re-read in the next mining session. Depending on the shape of the transaction, this produced either a spurious "Cannot apply undo change" warning or, more seriously, marked an earlier legitimate change such as the original INSERT as rolled back and silently dropped it from the change stream.

Rather than layering further fixes onto the existing logic, the LogMiner buffered implementation’s handling of partial rollbacks has been reworked around a much simpler rule. When a rollback-to-savepoint event is processed, the connector removes the most recent event with the matching row identifier from the transaction cache, along with any contiguous events with empty row identifiers immediately preceding it. This ensures the connector emits exactly the changes that survived the rollback.

No configuration changes are required. After upgrading, changes that were rolled back to a savepoint no longer reach downstream consumers, changes that were previously dropped in this scenario are emitted correctly, and the associated warnings no longer appear in the connector log. Any downstream compensation put in place to filter the spurious events can be removed. (dbz#1422, dbz#1914, dbz#1960)

Ehcache and Infinispan cache files must be removed when upgrading

Users who buffer Oracle transactions with Ehcache or Infinispan should remove their cache files as part of the upgrade, because the format of the cached data has changed in this release.

As a follow-up to the partial rollback rework described above, the bookkeeping that tracks the last enqueued event for each transaction moved from the streaming event source into the transaction cache. This simplifies the LogMiner buffered implementation, but it also alters the format of the serialized caches, so caches written by an earlier version no longer match what the connector expects.

No other behavior has changed as a result of this change. (dbz#2652)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium for MariaDB and MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for MariaDB and MySQL

Transient errors are retriable again

The MySQL and MariaDB connectors once again restart automatically after a transient failure, such as a dropped binlog connection or a brief network interruption. A regression introduced in Debezium 3.1 caused both connectors to classify every error as non-retriable, so these failures stopped the connector permanently and logged "This connector will be stopped" rather than triggering a restart.

The cause was in how the connectors' error handlers inspected an exception for non-retriable MySQL error codes. While walking the exception’s cause chain, the handler lost its reference to the original exception, so the built-in check that treats IOException and SQLException as communication errors never saw it and always answered that the error was not retriable. Only deployments that configured custom.retriable.exception were unaffected, as that check runs separately.

No configuration changes are required. After upgrading, transient communication errors are retried as expected, and any custom.retriable.exception setting added purely as a workaround can be removed. (dbz#2611)

Debezium for Oracle

ORA-02002 added to retriable exceptions for failover resilience

During an Oracle failover where multiple archive log destinations are configured, such as one for the primary and one for the standby, the connector could encounter an ORA-02002 error ("error while writing to audit trail"). Previously, this error was not recognized as retriable, causing the connector to stop unexpectedly rather than retrying the operation.

Debezium now includes ORA-02002 in its list of retriable Oracle exceptions, allowing the connector to automatically recover during failover transitions without requiring manual intervention. This is particularly beneficial for high-availability deployments where seamless failover handling is critical. (dbz#2625)

Other fixes

  • Savepoint partial rollback not handled when a LOB column changed (dbz#1735)

  • Rollback to savepoint discards more than it should when LOBs are enabled (dbz#1917)

  • Unbounded online-mode sessions and cap-growth heuristic inflation under sustained load in log-count mining (dbz#2326)

  • CREATE INDEX DDL fails to parse when using the ONLINE keyword (dbz#2484)

  • Handle ambiguous column name failures and use tran_end_time in lsn_time_mapping queries (dbz#2511)

  • Ambiguous partial rollback leaves a stale deferred transaction that pins the offset SCN for the full deferred retention (dbz#2531)

  • gRPC channels leaked on repeated connect, and close() throws an NPE when never connected (dbz#2545)

  • VGTID configuration compared with reference equality (==) instead of equals (dbz#2546)

  • Zero-day DATETIME values (e.g. 2024-01-00) crash the task; only zero-month values were handled (dbz#2548)

  • Agent running check fails the task with an IllegalStateException when the status query returns no rows (dbz#2551)

  • Irregular connector heartbeat intervals (dbz#2575)

  • CI job fails en masse when the first test suites run before server startup recovery completes (dbz#2585)

  • XStream metrics bean does not extend the MXBean interface (dbz#2602)

  • Log message mistakenly uses RowId rather than ThreadId (dbz#2617)

In total, 23 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.6.3.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Bhagyashree Goyal, Chijioke Ibekwe, Chris Cranford, Daniel Eriksson, Dario Rodrigues, Deniz Ozogul, Giovanni Panice, JerryS, Jiri Pechanec, Mario Fiore Vitale, Matthias Crauwels, Matt Langley, Minjae Lee, Robert Roldan, Sergei Nikolaev, and Vojtech Juranek!

entry.title: Supersonic Subatomic Debezium Server: Native builds with Quarkus and Mandrel

link.title: Supersonic Subatomic Debezium Server: Native builds with Quarkus and Mandrel

entry.content:
The Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2 release comes with a lot of changes, one of which is a complete rewrite of Debezium Server to support native builds with Quarkus and Mandrel. In this article, we’ll walk through creating a native distribution of Debezium Server and follow the steps from a previous article as an example.

Introduction

When we talk about native builds for Java Applications, we mean GraalVM, a high-performance runtime and toolchain for Java that was released by Oracle Labs in 2018. It extends the traditional Java platform with advanced compilation technologies, like ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation, enabling applications to be compiled into standalone executables with fast startup times and reduced memory consumption.

Building on these capabilities, Red Hat released the first version of Quarkus in 2019 Quarkus, designed to maximize build-time optimizations and minimize runtime overhead, making it one of the leading Java frameworks for native execution. By integrating closely with GraalVM Native Image, Quarkus lets applications achieve significant performance improvements over traditional JVM deployments.

To further support the Quarkus ecosystem, Red Hat introduced Mandrel in 2020, a downstream distribution of GraalVM focused specifically on native image generation for Quarkus applications.

The native distribution of Debezium Server leverages this ecosystem, combining Quarkus and Mandrel to deliver a lightweight, self-contained executable.

Gold for the Price of Silver: JIT Compilation in the Data Streaming Context

As mentioned before, AOT compilation is an approach in which machine code is generated before an application is executed, rather than during runtime. While AOT has long been used across many software ecosystems, it became a practical and widely adopted option for Java applications with the introduction of GraalVM Native Image.

By contrast, Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation has been a core part of Java’s execution model since the late 1990s. Sun introduced its first JIT compiler for Java in 1996, and the HotSpot JVM, released in 1999, further popularized adaptive runtime optimization by compiling frequently executed code paths into highly optimized machine code.

With JIT, Java applications start by running bytecode and gradually optimize themselves based on actual runtime behavior. This dynamic profiling enables excellent peak performance and throughput, making JIT the preferred choice for long-running services.

The trade-off between JIT and AOT depends on the target use case: JIT generally delivers higher maximum throughput for applications that run continuously and can benefit from runtime profiling and optimization. AOT, on the other hand, prioritizes operational efficiency, fast startup, and lower memory footprint at the cost of some runtime optimization opportunities.

Data streaming has traditionally been JIT territory: the JIT analyzes how code behaves during streaming and optimizes frequently executed methods, often called hot spots. Unlike AOT, the JIT can leverage runtime profiling to perform adaptive optimizations such as profile-guided inlining, speculative devirtualization, branch prediction tuning, and dynamic recompilation of hot code paths. These optimizations are continuously refined while the application is running, enabling the JVM to generate machine code tailored to real workload characteristics: the product of a well-established engineering effort spanning three decades.

The real price is the weight

The JVM runtime infrastructure and JIT compilation have a memory cost: a traditional HotSpot deployment requires memory not only for application data, but also for the JVM itself, including class metadata, dynamic class loading mechanisms, garbage collection metadata, profiling information, the JIT compiler, and the code cache that stores dynamically generated machine code. These components enable adaptive optimizations and high peak throughput, but they increase the overall memory footprint. Native executables generated with GraalVM Native Image or Mandrel remove much of this overhead by performing analysis and compilation at build time.

In this new era of rapidly increasing cloud costs driven by AI, optimizing memory consumption has become more important than ever.

The Hidden Gold of a Lost Age: Batch Ingestion

In some business scenarios, deploying a full ingestion and streaming platform capable of managing trillions of events in milliseconds is unnecessary. Sometimes the business simply needs to move data on an hourly or daily schedule from one source to another, without dealing with infrastructure complexity and costs. Debezium 3.6 introduced start/stop APIs for deterministic engine shutdown, which, combined with native builds, enable CDC pipelines for serverless environments. In this scenario, the native executable’s fast startup makes batch ingestion cost-effective in cloud environments.

A large ecosystem: why Quarkus

Currently, the Debezium community supports about 15 connectors for different data sources and 20 Debezium Server sinks. In addition, we maintain CDC-ready containers for testing, the Debezium Server operator, the Debezium Platform, and many other components that make our community vibrant and busy. Introducing native builds requires additional effort: Debezium’s own libraries and their dependencies must be compatible with native compilation — for example, classes accessed via reflection need to be registered with the compiler. Quarkus and its community maintain a large number of native-ready Java libraries, which makes adopting this layer significantly easier for our project.

Supported Connectors & Sinks

The following Debezium Connectors are supported for the native build in Debezium Server:

  • Postgres

  • MySQL

  • MariaDB

  • SQLServer

  • Oracle

  • MongoDB

and the following Debezium Server sinks:

  • Redis

  • HTTP

  • JDBC (not yet supported in native mode)

Please keep in mind that Debezium Server supports many other connectors and sinks in JVM mode.

Run Debezium Server

Following the example from the previous article, we can use Debezium Server to create a data integration pipeline from Postgres to Redis.

The example shown in this article is available in the debezium-examples repository.

We can start the source and target databases with the following Docker Compose file:

infrastructure-compose.yaml
services:

  postgres:
    container_name: postgres
    image: quay.io/debezium/example-postgres:3.6
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres
    networks:
      - backend

  redis:
    container_name: redis
    image: mirror.gcr.io/redis:7.0
    ports:
      - 6379:6379
    environment:
      - ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=yes
    networks:
      - backend

networks:
  backend:
    name: debezium-native-backend

Run the Docker Compose command below:

docker compose -f infrastructure-compose.yaml up -d

Once the source and target destination are healthy, you can start replicating your data with the following command:

 docker run --name inventory-pipeline -d \
    -v $(pwd)/application.properties:/debezium/config/application.properties:z \
    -p 8080:8080 \
    --network debezium-native-backend \
    quay.io/debezium/server-native:nightly

The configuration used is the following:

application.properties
# Debezium CDC configuration
debezium.source.offset.storage=org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.MemoryOffsetBackingStore
debezium.source.connector.class=io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
debezium.source.name=debezium
debezium.source.topic.prefix=migration
debezium.source.plugin.name=pgoutput
debezium.source.snapshot.mode=initial

# datasource configuration
debezium.source.offset.flush.interval.ms=0
debezium.source.database.hostname=postgres
debezium.source.database.port=5432
debezium.source.database.user=postgres
debezium.source.database.password=postgres
debezium.source.database.dbname=postgres
debezium.source.schema.include.list=inventory

# sink
debezium.sink.type=redis
debezium.sink.redis.address=redis:6379
debezium.sink.redis.cluster.enabled=false

quarkus.log.console.json=false

Similar to the previous article, you should see data flowing from Postgres to Redis. You can check the data has been correctly migrated to Redis:

docker exec -it redis redis-cli KEYS '*'

To inspect the replicated stream entries:

docker exec -it redis redis-cli XRANGE migration.inventory.customers - +
docker exec -it redis redis-cli XRANGE migration.inventory.products - +
docker exec -it redis redis-cli XRANGE migration.inventory.orders - +
docker exec -it redis redis-cli XRANGE migration.inventory.products_on_hand - +

Then let’s add a new customer:

docker exec -it postgres psql -U postgres -d postgres -c \
"INSERT INTO inventory.customers (first_name, last_name, email) VALUES ('John', 'Doe', 'john.doe@example.com');"

Performance Considerations

Performance evaluation is a serious thing. While we haven’t yet had time to perform a comprehensive performance analysis, the result is already clear: the memory footprint has been significantly reduced together with the startup time. You should notice a substantial decrease in the amount of memory used by Debezium Server with a speed-up in the startup. In the coming months, we will focus on evaluating Debezium Server’s performance under certain conditions and, based on the findings, continue improving it step by step.

What’s next

We are in the Beta stage and many things still need to be addressed. We plan to distribute binaries and support additional sinks for the native build in a future release. Additionally, the Debezium CLI project aims to integrate a simplified build process for Debezium Server that includes only the libraries required for a given pipeline (source and sink).

The future is bright for CDC!

entry.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2 Released

link.title: Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2 Released

entry.content:
As the leaves start to turn, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2, a release that delivers the first official release of the Milvus and SQLite source connectors and the Debezium CLI, alongside new capabilities across the platform, core library, and connectors.

Among the highlights, the Debezium Platform gains alerting, the reselect columns post processor gets a RocksDB-backed cache, a new embeddings transformation supports OpenAI models, and a rework of the JMX LastEvent metric rendering delivers improved snapshot throughput. Debezium Server adds TLS and mutual TLS support for the RabbitMQ Stream sink, and the JDBC sink can now map arrays to SingleStore JSON columns.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.7.0.Beta2

Debezium for Oracle

Savepoint partial rollbacks handled correctly

The Oracle connector handles a rollback to a savepoint by walking back through the buffered events of the transaction and discarding the change that was undone. Two defects in this process could cause the target to drift out of sync with the source.

First, when LOB support is enabled, the connector consolidates related INSERT and UPDATE events for the same row, but this consolidation only carried the column values forward and left the merged INSERT with a placeholder row identifier. When the partial rollback arrived, the connector could not find the event to discard, logged a "Cannot undo" warning, and emitted the rolled-back change that looked like a normal change to the target.

Second, when a rollback-to-savepoint event was mined near the end of a LogMiner session for a transaction that had not yet committed, the same rollback could be applied a second time when the transaction’s events were re-read in the next mining session. Depending on the shape of the transaction, this produced either a spurious "Cannot apply undo change" warning or, more seriously, marked an earlier legitimate change such as the original INSERT as rolled back and silently dropped it from the change stream.

The connector now preserves the correct row identifier when an UPDATE is folded into an INSERT, and partial rollbacks are applied idempotently so that a rollback already processed is never re-applied in a later mining session. Together these ensure the connector emits exactly the changes that survived the rollback.

No configuration changes are required. After upgrading, changes that were rolled back to a savepoint no longer reach downstream consumers, changes that were previously dropped in this scenario are emitted correctly, and the associated warnings no longer appear in the connector log. Any downstream compensation put in place to filter the spurious events can be removed. (dbz#1422, dbz#1914)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Operator

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium CLI

Debezium for CockroachDB

Debezium for Milvus

Debezium for Neo4j

Debezium for SQLite

Debezium Core

Embeddings SMT for OpenAI models

Debezium’s AI embeddings transformations gain a new module for OpenAI. Built on the LangChain4j OpenAI integration, the transformation sends the configured text field of each change event to an OpenAI embedding model and adds the resulting vector to the record.

This lets users who already standardize on OpenAI models enrich their change events with embeddings directly in the pipeline, alongside the existing embedding providers, without any custom code. (dbz#1067)

Dedicated metric for snapshot read events

Snapshot events are emitted with the READ operation, which previously had no dedicated counter in Debezium’s event metrics. As a result, monitoring dashboards in the Debezium Platform or in Prometheus showed zero create, update, and delete events while a snapshot was actively processing rows, making snapshot throughput effectively invisible.

Debezium now exposes a TotalNumberOfReadEventsSeen metric through JMX, following the same pattern as the existing create, update, and delete counters. The OpenTelemetry JMX configuration generated by the Debezium Operator maps the new attribute as a read event type, and the Debezium Platform gains a snapshot event count rate panel built on it. Note that the counter covers both initial and incremental snapshot events. (dbz#2167)

RocksDB cache for the reselect columns post processor

The ReselectColumnsPostProcessor re-queries the source database to replace unavailable value placeholders in events for TOASTed or LOB columns that the database does not include unless the column actually changed. An earlier improvement added a bounded, heap-based cache of previously reselected values to reduce the number of queries against the database.

This release introduces a standard cache contract that any storage backend can implement, and ships a RocksDB-based implementation out of the box. Cached column values can now live in persistent, disk-backed storage rather than being limited by JVM heap, allowing much larger working sets to be served from the cache and further reducing round trips to the source database. (dbz#2435)

Faster JMX LastEvent metric rendering improved snapshot throughput

The common pipeline metrics render a JSON summary of every dispatched change event to populate the JMX LastEvent attribute. Previously, each rendering constructed a brand new Jackson ObjectMapper, a cost paid for every snapshot and streaming event across all source connectors and both the Kafka Connect and Debezium Server runtimes.

The rendering now uses jackson-core’s stateless JsonStringEncoder, which is roughly seven times faster and allocates about five times less memory per event. In end-to-end snapshot benchmarks of a one million row table, this translated to up to 47% higher throughput on PostgreSQL and 38% on MySQL, with allocation per row roughly halved and noticeably fewer garbage collections and lower CPU usage. The rendered output is byte-identical to before and no new dependency is introduced. (dbz#2492)

Debezium for MongoDB

Date type keys in incremental snapshots

Incremental snapshots of MongoDB collections now support collections whose key is a BSON Date type. This continues the ongoing work to broaden the key types that can be used to chunk and resume MongoDB incremental snapshots, so collections keyed by dates no longer need a workaround to be captured incrementally. (dbz#765)

Debezium for MySQL

Accurate binlog positions beyond 4GB

The log_pos field in a MySQL binlog event header is an unsigned 32-bit value, yet a binlog file can legitimately grow beyond 4GB because MySQL never splits a transaction across files. Once a file crosses that boundary the server truncates the position it writes into the header, and the binlog client previously trusted that wrapped value. Every position the connector exposed past 4GB was therefore wrong, even though streaming itself continued: committed offsets, the source.pos field of emitted events, the reconnect position, and the BinlogPosition metric. On servers without GTIDs, a restart from a wrapped offset could land in the middle of an unrelated event and fail with the misleading "log event entry exceeded max_allowed_packet" error.

The binlog client now tracks the real 64-bit position itself, anchored on the 8-byte position carried by the ROTATE event and advanced by the length of each event read from the stream. Behavior for positions below 4GB is unchanged. Above it, offsets and source.pos now report the real position, consistent with what SHOW BINARY LOGS and mysqlbinlog report, and positions compare in the correct order. This change is complemented by the fix for the schema history comparator in dbz#2506.

One limitation remains: the binlog dump protocol itself only carries a 32-bit start position, so restarting from a position beyond 4GB on a server without GTIDs is still not possible. Tracking the real position removes the silent corruption and lays the groundwork for handling that case explicitly. (dbz#2508)

Debezium JDBC sink

SingleStore ARRAY to JSON mapping

The JDBC sink connector can now write Kafka Connect ARRAY schema values into SingleStore JSON columns. Array values arriving from Kafka topics are serialized to JSON on the way into the target column, so users no longer need a custom transformation or additional pre-processing to sink array fields into SingleStore. (dbz#2567)

Debezium Operator

Support for priorityClassName in the DebeziumServer pod template

The DebeziumServer custom resource’s pod template already exposed affinity, node selectors, tolerations, security context, and image pull secrets, but not a priority class. The pod template now accepts priorityClassName, so a Kubernetes priority class can be assigned to Debezium Server pods managed by the operator, allowing scheduling and preemption behavior to be controlled in the same way as other workloads in the cluster. (dbz#2251)

Image pull secrets for the operator Helm chart

The operator Helm chart already allowed the operator image to be overridden, but offered no way to attach an image pull secret to the operator pod itself. Deployments in clusters that cannot pull from public registries had to fork the chart or maintain hand-written manifests.

The chart now supports configuring imagePullSecrets for the operator deployment, completing the picture alongside the pull secret support that the DebeziumServer resource already provided for server pods. (dbz#2461)

Debezium Platform

Improved pipeline log viewer

The pipeline log screen in the Debezium Platform has received a series of usability improvements aimed at making large, fast-moving logs easier to work with. These include a proper loading state, the ability to pause and resume live log updates, and filtering by log level such as error, warning, info, and debug, so users can focus on the entries that matter when diagnosing a pipeline. (dbz#1380)

Image pull secrets and pull policy for all Helm chart images

The Debezium Platform Helm chart previously only allowed the image pull policy to be overridden for the conductor and stage images, and had no support for image pull secrets at all.

The chart now supports configuring imagePullPolicy for every image it deploys, including the descriptors and Debezium Server images, and introduces imagePullSecrets support with a hybrid model: a chart-level setting applies to all containers by default, and an optional per-component setting overrides it where needed. This makes the platform straightforward to deploy from private registries, in air-gapped environments, and across dev, staging, and production clusters with differing pull policies. All new fields are optional, so existing values files continue to work unchanged. (dbz#1851)

User-friendly names and descriptions for Debezium Server sink connectors

When listing Debezium Server sink connectors, the platform previously returned fully qualified implementation class names such as io.debezium.server.kinesis.KinesisChangeConsumer as both the connector name and description. Sink connectors now carry proper, human-readable names and descriptions, making them far easier to identify and select in the Platform UI. (dbz#1919)

MongoDB signal data collection verification

The conductor’s signal verification endpoint, used by the debezium source verify-signals CLI command, lets users confirm that a signal data collection is correctly set up for a source connection. For MongoDB connections this check was previously a stub that always reported success, so a misconfigured or non-existent signal collection went unnoticed.

The verification is now fully implemented for MongoDB sources, checking that the signal collection actually exists in the configured namespace. This brings MongoDB in line with the behavior already available for relational connections and makes the verification results trustworthy across all supported sources. (dbz#2270)

Alerting support

The Debezium Platform has offered pipeline monitoring through a set of predefined panels, but monitoring was passive: users had to watch dashboards to notice problems. Alerting closes this gap by letting users define threshold-based rules against existing monitoring panels and receive notifications when those thresholds are breached.

Alert rules are built by selecting a monitoring panel, a comparison operator, a numeric threshold, and an optional duration to suppress transient spikes. Rules are evaluated globally across all pipelines, and each alert identifies which pipeline triggered it. Alerts follow a pending, firing, and resolved lifecycle with incident tracking, support critical, warning, and info severity levels, and can be delivered via email over SMTP or an HTTP webhook in addition to always-on in-app visibility. A queryable, filterable alert history with configurable retention rounds out the feature.

The UI gains a new Alerts section with Rules, Channels, and History pages, plus a global alert badge in the header. Alert grouping, silencing, escalation policies, and repeat notifications are out of scope for this initial implementation. (dbz#2314)

Alerts in the Stage UI

The Stage user interface now surfaces alerts, giving users in-app visibility into alert rules, notification channels, and alert history. This is the user-facing counterpart to the alerting support introduced in dbz#2314. (dbz#2450)

Table explorer in the incremental snapshot action

Triggering an incremental snapshot from the Platform Stage previously required typing collection names by hand. The incremental snapshot action now embeds the same table explorer component already used in the source configuration, so users can browse and select the tables or collections to snapshot using the existing collection API rather than entering identifiers manually. (dbz#2465)

All pipeline statuses shown in the Stage UI

The Platform Stage previously only distinguished the failed state for a pipeline. With the conductor now reporting additional states such as deploying and running, the Stage UI displays the full set of pipeline statuses, giving users a clearer picture of where each pipeline is in its lifecycle at a glance. (dbz#2543)

Debezium Server

Connection validator for RocketMQ

The Debezium Platform can now verify connections to Apache RocketMQ before a pipeline is deployed. A dedicated connection validator, connection type, and schema have been added for RocketMQ, so users get immediate feedback on misconfigured hosts or credentials rather than discovering the problem when the pipeline starts. (dbz#1094)

TLS and mTLS support for the RabbitMQ Stream sink

The RabbitMQ Stream sink previously had no way to configure TLS, so connecting to a TLS-enabled stream port failed with a closed connection as the client sent plaintext to the encrypted endpoint.

The rabbitmqstream sink now supports TLS and mutual TLS, with configurable trust and client certificate material and hostname verification, bringing it to parity with the TLS support already available in the AMQP-based RabbitMQ sink. This allows Debezium Server to publish to RabbitMQ Stream clusters that enforce encrypted, certificate-authenticated connections, a common requirement in Kubernetes deployments. (dbz#1582)

Debezium CLI

First official release of the Debezium CLI

Until now, creating, managing, and monitoring change data capture pipelines outside of Kafka Connect meant working through the Debezium Platform user interface or its REST API. With this release, the Debezium CLI has its first official release, giving developers and operators a single command-line entry point for the whole pipeline lifecycle, whether they are iterating locally or automating production workflows.

The CLI is distributed through JBang and is organized around two subsystems. The platform subsystem talks to a running Debezium Platform and provides commands to list, create, update, and delete pipelines, sources, destinations, connections, and transforms, to stream pipeline logs, send signals, and verify signal configuration, and to switch between multiple platform environments. The build subsystem lets users scaffold a configuration, assemble a trimmed Debezium Server distribution containing only the connector and sink they need, wrap it in an OCI container image without a Docker daemon, and push the image to a registry.

Together these allow a user to go from an empty terminal to a running pipeline without hand-managing JAR files or configuration. (dbz#1955)

Debezium for CockroachDB

CockroachDB connector graduates from incubating

The CockroachDB connector has carried an incubating designation since its first release. With this release the connector graduates from incubating status: the incubating notices have been removed from the connector README and reference documentation, and the connector’s plugin archive no longer carries the incubating suffix in the installation guide.

If the incubating status kept you from adopting the connector, now is the time to take another look: the CockroachDB connector is production-ready. (dbz#2580)

Debezium for Milvus

Incubating Milvus source connector

Milvus is an open-source vector database built for storing, indexing, and searching high-dimensional embeddings at scale, and it sits at the heart of many retrieval-augmented generation and semantic search systems. Debezium has supported Milvus as a sink for some time, and this release adds the other direction: an incubating source connector that captures inserts, updates, and deletes from Milvus collections in real time.

Milvus does not expose a change stream through its API, so the connector reads directly from the internal message queue channels that Milvus publishes every write to, resolving collection schemas through the Milvus metadata API and using etcd checkpoints and timestamp-oracle ordering to provide resumable, correctly ordered events. Change events carry full schema fidelity, including vector field dimensions, so downstream consumers can replicate embeddings to other stores, keep search indexes in sync, or feed AI pipelines. The connector supports an initial snapshot of existing collections with a seamless hand-off to streaming, heartbeats, notifications, and metrics.

The connector requires Milvus 2.5 or later deployed with Kafka as the message queue backend. As an incubating connector, its configuration and behavior may still change in future releases. (dbz#2065)

Debezium for Neo4j

Hardening of the Neo4j source SMT

The Neo4j source single message transformation has been hardened with improved fail safety and observability, making it more resilient to unexpected input and easier to monitor in production. (dbz#2574)

Debezium for SQLite

Incubating SQLite source connector

SQLite is the most widely deployed database engine in the world, embedded in browsers, mobile and desktop applications, and a growing number of edge and IoT devices, and increasingly used as a primary application database. Until now it has been one of the most common sources of data with no standard way to stream its changes, and this release closes that gap with an incubating Debezium source connector for SQLite.

The connector brings Debezium’s familiar pipeline to a SQLite database file: an initial snapshot of existing table data followed by continuous streaming of inserts, updates, and deletes. Because SQLite has no server process or transaction log to tap into, changes are captured through a change data capture log table that database triggers keep up to date, which the connector then reads and translates into standard Debezium change events with the usual envelope and source metadata. Table and column include and exclude filters and offset-based resume after a restart are supported, and the connector runs against the standard sqlite-jdbc driver with no external services required.

As an incubating connector, its configuration and behavior may still change in future releases. (dbz#2056)

Other fixes

  • MongoDB validation should not report success when the instance is not configured as a replica set (dbz#414)

  • Unify XStream behavior with LogMiner when using DBMS_LOB methods (dbz#579)

  • Multi-partition streaming metrics expose CapturedTables from all partitions (dbz#586)

  • Add connection validator for Milvus (dbz#1097)

  • Restart the connector or throw an exception when the TCP connection remains established but the MySQL session is dead (dbz#1474)

  • MySQL CDC fails due to TIMESTAMP schema drift (Zoned to Nano) (dbz#1550)

  • Error while attempting to set resume token: "No value present" (dbz#1643)

  • Savepoint partial rollback not handled when a LOB column changed (dbz#1735)

  • Rollback to savepoint discards more than it should when LOBs are enabled (dbz#1917)

  • Data loss in direct mode on update with fetch size greater than zero (dbz#2012)

  • Implement the host agent, a lightweight remote-side HTTP service for host deployments (dbz#2094)

  • Implement Ansible-based pipeline deployment service for host deployments (dbz#2101)

  • Build subsystem for Debezium build and OCI image assembly (dbz#2241)

  • NPE in conductor when signal data collection verification is called without a table name (dbz#2271)

  • Log-count mining: unbounded online-mode sessions under sustained load and cap-growth heuristic inflating on slow passes (dbz#2326)

  • Support pipeline statuses other than FAILED (dbz#2351)

  • Fix smart editor in the source and destination creation (dbz#2385)

  • Native build is broken for JDBC sink due to missing dialect (dbz#2416)

  • Implement real-time stream synchronization, vector store idempotency, and live visual dashboard (dbz#2423)

  • Create common core assembly package for embedded runtime (dbz#2466)

  • inherit.epoch validation reports problems but never fails (dbz#2479)

  • vitess.grpc.headers silently drops headers whose value contains a colon (dbz#2480)

  • TimescaleDB transform connection issues are not retriable (dbz#2490)

  • Configuration.getList(Field) ignores the field’s default value, unlike getString and getInteger (dbz#2493)

  • Error processing CDC data stream with CLOB after LVARCHAR or NVARCHAR (dbz#2502)

  • Binlog history comparator does not handle positions beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE (dbz#2506)

  • Handle "Ambiguous column name" failures and use tran_end_time in lsn_time_mapping usage (dbz#2511)

  • Missing dependency and build assembly for Debezium Server custom distribution profile (dbz#2514)

  • format.header option only accepts json (dbz#2520)

  • Fail when no child partitions are received (dbz#2523)

  • NullPointerException for enum with no values (dbz#2525)

  • Stage: signal collection modal shows SQL DDL for MongoDB sources (dbz#2527)

  • Stop annotation (debezium.io/stop) does not trigger reconciliation (dbz#2528)

  • Ambiguous partial rollback leaves stale deferred transaction that pins the offset SCN for the full deferred retention (dbz#2531)

  • gRPC channels leaked on repeated connect, and close() throws NPE when never connected (dbz#2545)

  • VGTID configuration compared with reference equality instead of equals (dbz#2546)

  • Zero-day DATETIME values (e.g. 2024-01-00) crash the task; only zero-month was handled (dbz#2548)

  • Agent running check fails the task with IllegalStateException when the default query returns no rows (dbz#2551)

entry.title: Debezium 3.6.2.Final Released

link.title: Debezium 3.6.2.Final Released

entry.content:
As summer winds down, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.2.Final, a maintenance release packed with correctness, performance, and security improvements across the entire connector family.

Among the highlights, incremental snapshots now work on PostgreSQL read-only replicas, and a fix to Debezium’s internal caching keeps long-running connectors from gradually losing throughput. On the security front, Debezium Server now masks passwords in its logs, and the PostgreSQL JDBC driver has been bumped to 42.7.13 to address CVE-2026-54291. Rounding things out are a healthy batch of DDL parser fixes for MySQL and Oracle, data-correctness fixes for incremental snapshots and heartbeat error handling, and improved PostgreSQL parallel snapshot consistency.

Read on for the full details!

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Container Images

Debezium Core

Fix for gradual throughput loss in long-running connectors

Connectors could slowly lose throughput the longer they ran, with no errors logged and no change in workload to explain it. One production deployment saw its rate fall from roughly 90K records per minute at startup to 12,500 after eighteen hours, with a single thread consuming nearly a full CPU core.

The cause was in BoundedConcurrentHashMap, the fixed-size cache Debezium uses across the runtime for schemas, topic names, prepared statements, and similar lookups. Its internal housekeeping ran when an entry was read, but not when an entry already in the cache was overwritten, so a caller that only ever writes never triggered it, and an internal tracking list grew without bound. Checking the length of that list also became more expensive as it grew, so the cost of processing each record climbed along with it.

Writes now trigger the same housekeeping that reads always have, and the list length is tracked as it changes rather than recounted on every access. Cache sizes, eviction behavior, and the entries retained are all unchanged. (dbz#2255)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Incremental snapshots on read-only replicas

Incremental snapshots on PostgreSQL read-only replicas previously failed with cannot execute pg_current_xact_id() during recovery error, because the snapshot logic attempted to create a new transaction ID, which is not permitted on replicas. This caused connectors running with read.only=true to enter an infinite restart loop when an incremental snapshot was triggered.

This has been corrected, and users running against a hot standby can now use incremental snapshots for re-snapshotting subsets of data without restarting the connector or switching to the primary. (dbz#1080, dbz#2431)

Container Images

PostgreSQL GUC logical decoder support

A recent PostgreSQL security update for PostgreSQL 15 and later introduces a new output_plugin_libraries GUC setting that restricts which logical decoding output plugins can start. By default, PostgreSQL now permits only pgoutput and test_decoding, so any updated PostgreSQL instance, including publicly available container images, will reject the decoderbufs plugin.

The Debezium PostgreSQL container images now explicitly configure this GUC to include decoderbufs alongside the default plugins. For users who have not yet migrated to pgoutput and continue to use decoderbufs, the output_plugin_libraries setting must be specified in the PostgreSQL server configuration to include decoderbufs. (dbz#2434)

Other fixes

  • Fix multiple MySQL DDL parser errors (dbz#360 dbz#690 dbz#2381)

  • Passwords are not masked in Debezium Server log output (dbz#1201)

  • JDBC storage RetriableConnection retries a failing operation indefinitely without honoring max.retries (dbz#2244)

  • OpenLineage SMT never emits dataset metadata for schema changes on known topics and writes to its dedup caches on every record (dbz#2262)

  • Fix incremental snapshots stopping after the database closes the connection (dbz#2275)

  • Incorrect span attribute mapping for type in the Quarkus outbox extension (dbz#2286)

  • Fix PostgreSQL parallel snapshot producing inconsistent reads across pooled connections (dbz#2330)

  • Upgrade Hibernate to 7.2.19 (dbz#2331)

  • Upgrade MongoDB driver to 5.9.2 (dbz#2332, dbz#2449)

  • Incremental snapshot silently loses data on NUMERIC keys holding NaN or Infinity (dbz#2333)

  • Temporals.max/min give incorrect results for sub-second durations with equal whole seconds (dbz#2338)

  • Upgrade Quarkus to 3.33.2 (dbz#2344)

  • Fix Oracle LogMiner client ID exclusion filter not handling null values (dbz#2348)

  • Fix Oracle LogMiner extended string parser failing on table aliases (dbz#2366)

  • Fix duplicated Oracle LogMiner extended string and XML values (dbz#2368)

  • Snapshot failure for array values when using the AWS Advanced JDBC driver (dbz#2387)

  • Upgrade PostgreSQL JDBC driver to 42.7.13 (CVE-2026-54291) (dbz#2400)

  • Fix multiple Oracle DDL parser errors (dbz#2405 dbz#2407)

  • Fix config validation errors being masked by HTTP 500 NullPointerException on Kafka Connect (dbz#2415)

  • unavailable.value.placeholder applies to text but not to varchar(max), nvarchar(max), or varbinary(max) (dbz#2420)

  • Connector incorrectly parses text defaults containing escaped single quotes (dbz#2440)

  • MathOps.add drops the first operand for BigInteger overloads (dbz#2446)

  • SQL syntax error on Oracle 11g during boundary queries due to unsupported OFFSET…​FETCH clause (dbz#2448)

  • JDBC sink omits OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE causing failure on PostgreSQL GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY primary keys (dbz#2459)

  • NullPointerException in heartbeat error handlers when the driver reports no SQL state (dbz#2464)

  • Username/client filters have no effect when tracking is disabled (dbz#2473)

  • Chunked parallel initial snapshot does not apply snapshot.fetch.size to chunk statements (dbz#2483)

  • Add ORA-02399 as an allowed Oracle retriable exceptions (dbz#2487)
